text.p: Europe's car manufacturers and oil refining companies clashed on Thursday over whose job it should be to meet new European Union standards aimed at cutting air pollution.
The European Commission worked closely with the car and oil industries to draw up limits on pollutants, applicable from 2000, which satisfied both sectors.
But pressure from the European Parliament to tighten the 2000 standards and bring in even stricter measures in 2005 has put a strain on relations.

"If by disaster we get stronger figures for 2000 we expect the effort to come from the oil industry," Georges Douin, carmaker Renault's senior vice president, told a conference on refining, vehicle technology and fuel quality.

Douin said the motor industry was working on cleaner, more fuel efficient engines but insisted its efforts to cut pollutant emissions such as nitrogen oxides would not be effective unless the oil industry came up with cleaner, less sulphurous fuels.
But oil giant Total's senior executive Jean-Paul Vettier said cutting the sulphur and aromatics in fuels would cost a fortune and actually increase emissions of greenhouse gases.

"These investments would cause much higher refinery energy consumption and...would almost double the CO2 emissions, representing an annual increase of 30 million tonnes of CO2," Vettier said, calling for future anti-pollution measures to focus on improving vehicle technology and urban traffic flows.

Douin questioned the oil industry's calculation that it would cost $50 billion to produce optimal motor fuels, saying the cost of improvements could be passed on to consumers through increases in petrol and diesel prices.
EU environment ministers are due on June 19-20 to examine the draft EU rules for fuel and engine standards for 2000.
The EU's executive Commission has pledged to follow up this initiative with a new study on anti-pollution measures in 1998, which could lead to plans for tighter emissions laws in 2005.

Both Renault and Total accepted the need for the new study but they queried whether new mandatory limits would be needed in 2005 and urged the Commission to target national car tax policies rather than industry in future.
Douin praised Germany's plans to bring in higher rates of ownership tax for older, more polluting cars, and urged other countries in the 15-member EU bloc to follow suit.
Replacing old cars would help reduce the European car industry's 30 percent overcapacity rate, he said.
But on Wednesday, the head of the Commission's oil unit, Johannes Maters, told the conference the burden for future anti-pollution measures lay with industry.

The Commission's new Auto/Oil study would look at possible tax incentives but if would be an uphill battle to get the member states to accept EU-wide tax proposals, he warned. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
